title: Worksheet — Power-sharing (Class 10 CBSE Civics)
instructions: Attempt all 11 questions. Show your reasoning where required. Total time: 50 minutes.

questions.question: Sri Lanka emerged as an independent country in:
Belgium amended its constitution four times between 1970 and 1993.
In 1956, Sri Lanka recognised ____ as the only official language.
Power shared among legislature, executive and judiciary is:
Why is 'tyranny of the majority' bad even for the majority itself?
options: it undermines national unity and brings ruin to the majority too in the long run
questions.answer: it undermines national unity and brings ruin to the majority too in the long run

questions.question: Describe the ethnic composition of Sri Lanka.
questions.answer: Sri Lanka has two major social groups: SINHALA-speakers (74%) and TAMIL-speakers (18%). Tamils are further split into Sri Lankan Tamils (13%, native) and Indian Tamils (5%, plantation workers). Most Sinhalese are BUDDHIST; most Tamils are HINDU or MUSLIM. About 7% are CHRISTIANS, drawn from both communities.

questions.question: List four key features of Belgium's power-sharing model.
questions.answer: (i) EQUAL Dutch / French ministers in the central government; some laws need majority support of each language group. (ii) Strong STATE GOVERNMENTS (Flemish + Walloon) that are NOT subordinate to the centre. (iii) BRUSSELS has its own government with EQUAL representation of both communities. (iv) A 'COMMUNITY GOVERNMENT' for each language community handles culture, education and language matters.

questions.question: What is the difference between PRUDENTIAL and MORAL reasons for power-sharing?
questions.answer: PRUDENTIAL reasons stress that power-sharing brings BETTER OUTCOMES — it reduces conflict between social groups, prevents violence and ensures political stability. It is based on careful calculation of gains and losses. MORAL reasons say that power-sharing is the VERY SPIRIT of democracy itself — people have a right to be consulted on how they are governed.

questions.question: Compare the Belgian and Sri Lankan approaches to managing ethnic diversity. What lessons do they teach about power-sharing?
questions.answer: Both Belgium and Sri Lanka are small countries with sharp ethnic and linguistic divisions, but they took OPPOSITE paths. SRI LANKA — adopted MAJORITARIAN measures: a 1956 Sinhala-only law, preferential job and university policies for Sinhalese, and a constitution that fostered Buddhism. The Tamil minority was alienated; their demand for autonomy was repeatedly denied; by the 1980s they demanded a separate Tamil EELAM. The country slid into a CIVIL WAR that ended only in 2009, after thousands of deaths and massive damage. BELGIUM — RECOGNISED its diversity and amended the constitution four times between 1970 and 1993 to share power: equal Dutch–French ministers in the central government; strong state governments not subordinate to the centre; equal representation in Brussels; and a unique COMMUNITY GOVERNMENT for cultural / language matters elected by each language community. The arrangements are complicated, but they have AVOIDED civic strife — Brussels even became the EU capital. LESSONS: (i) majoritarianism may look attractive in the short run but undermines national unity and hurts the majority too; (ii) carefully designed power-sharing — even if complicated — produces stable democracies; (iii) constitutional and institutional arrangements matter more than slogans of unity.

questions.question: 'Power-sharing is the very spirit of democracy.' Discuss this statement with examples of horizontal, vertical, social-group and party power-sharing.
questions.answer: Democracy means rule by the people — and the people are not one undivided block but a collection of social groups, regions and interests. So power-sharing is not just one feature of democracy among many; it IS democracy. Without it, an elected government can quickly become tyrannical. There are at least four forms: (i) HORIZONTAL — among legislature, executive and judiciary (checks and balances). E.g. in India the Supreme Court can strike down laws of Parliament; the executive is answerable to the Lok Sabha. (ii) VERTICAL — between Union, State and Local governments, with the Constitution clearly assigning different powers to each. (iii) Among SOCIAL GROUPS — the Belgian Community Government; reserved seats for SCs and STs in Indian assemblies. (iv) Among POLITICAL PARTIES, pressure groups and movements — coalition governments; trade unions and business associations and farmer movements influencing policy. PRUDENTIAL reasons (avoiding conflict, ensuring stability) AND MORAL reasons (people have a right to be consulted) both support power-sharing. Sri Lanka shows what happens when power is hoarded by the majority; Belgium shows what is possible when it is shared.
